Sara — thanks for the clear list. High level answers upfront, then a short proposed MAP: 

1) Credits mapping: our Optimize recommendations (batching/caching/quantization suggestions) are evaluated per-run and then applied in the serving plane. For your workload size (~75k tokens/day) the pilot spend projection is: ~2.2M tokens consumed (including test & debug). Roughly: 1 credit = 1,000 model tokens for hosted Optimize evals. For the pilot we typically offer a 10k-credit onboarding package that covers evaluation runs + the first two weeks of applied savings measurement.

2) Quantization: for a Llama-3 7B variant we recommend starting with int8 (AQ8) for production parity and faster iteration; consider 4-bit (Q4_0) for latency-sensitive inference if you can accept a small quality check. Lauren (cc'd) will drop a short technical note with throughput/latency tradeoffs and a sample quantization checklist.

3) Commercials/pilot structure: we do three common approaches — 30-day proof-of-value (POV) with 10k credits + optional usage billing, a matched-credit pilot (customer buys a small credit pack and we match 50%), or a time-limited credit grant if the customer is strategic. For Nimbus I recommend the matched-credit pilot: reduces procurement friction, aligns incentives, and gives us an on-boarded billing relationship. If you convert to a 6-month reserved commit within 60 days we can offer a 20% discount on token pricing and an additional 5k credit bonus.

Attached is a short SOW template and a pilot credit summary. Lauren — can you add the quantization table and recommended batch-window settings? Mina, Markus — can you weigh in on Dedicated vs hosted capacity recommendations for Nimbus (they mentioned latency SLO in procurement).

Proposed next steps (quick):

Hi Sara — short technical note to supplement Connor's commercial overview. I kept it concise so procurement can copy into the SOW: 

Summary recommendations for Llama-3 7B variant (pilot):
- Start: int8 (AQ8) for inference to preserve accuracy; this reduces GPU memory by ~2x vs fp16 and typically lowers cost 30–45% depending on kernel set.
- If latency target < 40ms p50 on single-request traffic, evaluate Q4_0 with per-layer calibration. Q4_0 can cut per-token compute ~20–35% further but needs an automated QA pass (prompt sets) to catch regressions.
- Batching: use a dynamic batching window of 8–20ms with a max batch size of 32 for your 75k tokens/day profile. That balances latency and throughput — in our tests it yielded ~3–5x throughput uplift vs single-shot while keeping p95 tail small.
- Prefix/KV cache: enable prefix cache for conversational flows where >30% of tokens are repeated context. Set TTL at 10 minutes for session-intensive features; for one-off queries set TTL to 0 (no caching).
- Autoscaler: for a pilot, hosted with burstable Dedicated cap is easiest. If you require strict isolation and predictable latency under peak load (e.g., 500 concurrent sessions), Dedicated GPUs with pinned pools are recommended. Markus can share rough node counts if you can share peak RPS.

Quality guardrails we recommend during pilot:
- Baseline evaluation set: 250 prompts across key flows for regressions.
- Automated A/B harness: run new quantized variant vs baseline for key prompts and flag >1.5% accuracy drift.

I've attached a short workbook that maps throughput/latency to expected token burn under the three quant configs (fp16 / int8 / q4). See quant-reco-v1.xlsx.

Happy to hop on a short 30-min technical session to align implementation with your infra.

Lauren Bishop
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
(Attachment: quant-reco-v1.xlsx)
